title: The cleanup that uninstalled the network
role: You are one of the admins of a public OpenStack cloud hosting hundreds of community projects on Debian VMs, all managed by Puppet. Today you lead the response.

source.label: Wikimedia: Incidents/2023-09-29 CloudVPS vms losing network connectivity

brief: Friday, 07:06 UTC. You start work and notice the alerting system is down. On IRC, users have reported connection problems since 04:14, and one opened an outage task at 06:56. No page reached anyone.

steps.situation: Your dashboards are quiet. Users say their tools are unreachable.

choices.text: Treat the silence as a symptom: check the monitoring stack itself and reproduce a user report
choices.why: The monitoring VMs were hit too, so nothing could alert. The front proxy for all projects is unresponsive: that's a platform outage, not one user's tool.

choices.text: No alerts, so it's the users' own projects
choices.why: Monitoring that is down sends no alerts. Silence from it proves nothing.

choices.text: Restart the alerting server and wait for its alerts
choices.why: It shares the fault, so it may not come back, and you lose time you could spend on the real fault.

steps.situation: On a VM that still works you check its network setup, then its package log.
steps.evidence:
$ command -v dhclient || echo missing
missing
$ grep -B3 'Remove: isc-dhcp-client' /var/log/apt/history.log
Start-Date: 2023-09-28  11:38:40
Commandline: /usr/bin/apt-get -q -y remove isc-dhcp-client
Remove: isc-dhcp-client:amd64

choices.text: Read it: Puppet removed the DHCP client yesterday; VMs drop off as their leases expire
choices.why: Found by 07:18: a package cleanup in Puppet removed `isc-dhcp-client` from bullseye VMs. A working VM is just one whose lease hasn't run out yet.

choices.text: Rebuild the broken VMs from images
choices.why: Hundreds of VMs, their data, and a Puppet run that removes the client again.
With no DHCP client they boot without an address, and the ones that still work lose theirs.

steps.situation: You merge the revert at 07:23. But broken VMs can't reach the Puppet server, so they will never pick it up.

choices.text: Two tracks at once: one admin scripts the fix for the whole fleet, another repairs core VMs by hand; email the users' announce list
choices.why: What was done. Monitoring alerts came back by hand at 08:21, the script ran over the fleet from 08:35, and the first email went out at 07:31.

choices.text: Wait for the Puppet agents to apply the revert
choices.why: An agent without network can't fetch the revert. You'd wait forever.

choices.text: Fix VMs one by one by hand, starting with whoever complains loudest
choices.why: Too slow for a fleet, and in the wrong order: monitoring and the proxies serve everyone.

steps.situation: Networking is back, but NFS clients hang: Kubernetes workers and grid nodes have stuck mounts. The NFS server's network setup needs a reboot and a Puppet run.

choices.text: Reboot in order: the NFS servers first, then the clients with stuck handles, in batches
choices.why: The NFS server was rebooted at 09:32, the Kubernetes workers from 09:37, and all grid nodes by 10:08. The grid reboot cookbook failed on stuck nodes because it doesn't force a reboot.
Clients that come up before the NFS server hang again, and every hosted tool restarts at once.

choices.text: Wait for the NFS mounts to recover by themselves
choices.why: In this setup they don't. Stuck handles need the reboot.

steps.situation: All services back at 11:46 on 29 September. Users found the outage before you did. What goes into the follow-up?

choices.text: Fix paging, monitor the monitoring, build a console cookbook, make NFS recover without reboots, roll package removals to a canary group first
choices.why: The first four are the report's actions. A canary group is the general lesson: a removal you test on a few VMs fails there first.
Puppet is also how you fix the fleet. Make changes safer, not rare.

choices.text: Find out who merged the cleanup and restrict their access
choices.why: A routine cleanup did this; the gaps were no staging, no meta-monitoring and pages that went nowhere.

debrief.what_happened: At 11:07 UTC on 28 September 2023 a Puppet package-cleanup change was merged that removed `isc-dhcp-client` (which provides `dhclient`) from Debian 11 bullseye VMs on Cloud VPS. As DHCP leases expired, VMs lost their network: Toolforge, PAWS, Quarry and the external proxies went down, and so did the metricsinfra monitoring VMs, so no alert fired. NFS clients got stuck. Users reported problems on IRC from 04:14 on 29 September; at 07:06 an admin noticed Alertmanager was down, at 07:16 `dhclient` was found missing, and at 07:18 apt logs pointed at Puppet. The revert went in at 07:23, but Puppet could not run on broken VMs, so admins fixed them by hand and with a fleet script. NFS servers, Kubernetes workers and grid nodes were rebooted, and all services were back at 11:46 on 29 September. Actions: find out why no pages went out, meta-monitoring for metricsinfra, a cookbook to run commands through `virsh console`, and NFS that recovers without a reboot and Puppet run.
lessons: No alerts is not good news until you've checked the alerting.
Package removals are changes: test them on a canary group.
When config management can't reach hosts, a revert fixes nothing: have an out-of-band path.
Recover in dependency order: monitoring and shared services first, NFS servers before clients.
